yarn-troppo.meaning: Keeps every beat, including the ambiguous towel line ("might've put a bit of this on, too"), but adds a few invented touches: "not one to take the Sheriff's word for it", "every last one of 'em", and overstates Mrs Peters's worry as "She was beside herself about that".
yarn-troppo.sense: Terms mostly fit: "stickybeak", "Not much chop as a housekeeper", "Farmers' wives are flat out", "spick and span". "Yeah, but nah, I don't mean anything by it" strains as a rendering of a flat "No", and "kicked all over the shop" makes the shoved pans scattered.
yarn-troppo.authenticity: Much is natural ("Grotty towels!", "give his mitts a wash", "Seems a bit low to rubbish her"), but some stock bolt-ons: "having a Captain Cook round" for a stage direction, "Nothin' here, mate", and "laying on the charm like a young pollie after your vote".
yarn-troppo.register: A full level-4 retelling, slang in nearly every line; swearing stays at dad level ("Sweet bugger-all", "her bloody preserves", "too flamin' well"). If anything a shade heavy in the stage directions ("Not a flicker.").
yarn-troppo.tone: The men's condescension and the women's quiet stiffness survive ("stiff as a board", "the women don't crack a smile"), but "get their knickers in a twist over trifles" and the jokey asides tip the scene a little toward comedy.
yarn-troppo.flow: Reads well aloud in the dialogue ("I'd like to pick that up with you a bit later"); a few padded stage directions ("shoulder to shoulder", "smooth as you like") slow it.
yarn-troppo.variety: Wide range with little repetition: "squiz", "stickybeak", "geek", "mitts", "flat out", "picking holes in everything", "rubbish her".
yarn-troppo.essence: Unmistakably the Trifles kitchen scene; keeps "trifles" ("knickers in a twist over trifles") and the towel thread through to "Wish I'd thought of that sooner."

unharnessed.meaning: Every beat survives in order: the frozen fruit, "a bit more serious than jam to worry about", the towels, the neighbour questions, "keep an eye out for anything that might come in handy for us". "might've put a bit of this muck on it himself" makes the deputy-dirtied-towel reading explicit but correct. "Job's fair enough" for "Duty's all right" is a small shift.
unharnessed.sense: Terms fit their contexts: "Not much chop as a housekeeper", "a fair whack of work", "grubby awful quick", "lie of the land", "bagging her". "her jam" for preserves narrows bottled fruit to jam.
unharnessed.authenticity: Sounds like Australians talking: "wouldn't it rot your socks", "the women don't give an inch", "Seems a bit rough, bagging her". Nothing reads as tourist stock.
unharnessed.register: Solidly Aussie throughout without overloading, one "bloody mess" and nothing stronger: about level 4, vulgarity 1. Some lines stay close to the original ("Yes, Mr Henderson.").
unharnessed.tone: The quiet tension is intact: "laying on the charm like a young pollie", "(_stiffly_) There's a fair whack of work to be done on a farm", "No, I don't mean anything."
unharnessed.flow: Smooth throughout; only "Well, wouldn't it rot your socks, women!" is a slightly awkward join.
unharnessed.variety: Varied ("squiz", "hops up", "fussin'", "mates", "traipsing"), though "bagging" comes twice: "bagging everything" and "bagging her".
unharnessed.essence: Clearly the original scene, keeping "fussin' over trifles" and the towel thread to "Wish I'd thought of that earlier."

dinkum-3.meaning: Mostly faithful, but the towel line is reversed: "could've given this a wipe while he was at it" says the deputy should have cleaned the towel, where the original suggests he dirtied it. "fussing over little things" also drops the word "trifles".
dinkum-3.sense: Most terms fit ("Not much chop", "schmick", "shot through", "stickybeaking"), but "Yeah, righto, Mr Henderson" turns Mrs Peters's dutiful "Yes" into casual assent, and "Yeah, but nah" strains for a flat "No".
dinkum-3.authenticity: Natural, modern Aussie mostly: "Seems a bit rough, bagging her for not having the place schmick". Some stock: "have a Captain Cook round the kitchen", "Yeah, but nah".
dinkum-3.register: Level 4 weight, slang in most lines, one "Sweet bugger-all" for swearing: on the brief.
dinkum-3.tone: Tension largely held, but Mrs Peters's "Yeah, righto, Mr Henderson" loses her deference, and the reversed towel line loses Mrs Hale's quiet defence of Mrs Wright.
dinkum-3.flow: Reads smoothly: "Only I don't reckon having John Wright about would make a place any cheerier."
dinkum-3.variety: Good range, though "mitts" comes twice ("washes his mitts", "Men's mitts") and "bagging" twice.
dinkum-3.essence: Recognisable, but losing "trifles" (the play's title and point) and the deputy turn flattens what the scene is about.

yarn-dinkum.meaning: Faithful line by line: "might've got a bit of this on" keeps the deputy hint, "stewin' over trifles" keeps the key word, and nothing is invented.
yarn-dinkum.sense: Terms fit: "the women don't thaw", "Not much chop as a housekeeper", "have a go at her", "grotty awful quick". Only "Yeah, but nah, I don't mean anything" strains.
yarn-dinkum.authenticity: Natural throughout ("sticking their noses in and picking holes in everything", "Seems a bit rough to have a go at her"); "Yeah, but nah" is the one stock tic.
yarn-dinkum.register: Lighter than level 4: many lines stay near the original ("I want to get the lay of things upstairs now", "And why's that? You didn't like her?"). Vulgarity right ("Sweet bugger-all", "flamin' well").
yarn-dinkum.tone: The tension and Mrs Hale's stiffness come through whole: "(_stiffly_) There's heaps of work to be done on a farm."
yarn-dinkum.flow: Reads cleanly; "kicks his foot against the pans" is kept a little stiffly from the original.
yarn-dinkum.variety: Fair range ("squiz", "mitts", "grotty", "traipsing") with no tic repeated, though the light touch gives it less to vary.
yarn-dinkum.essence: Unmistakably the original: "Wish I'd thought of that sooner. Seems a bit rough to have a go at her".

engine.meaning: Mostly the original text with inserts; "what would we do without the ladies, mate?" and "Farmers' wives have their mitts full" garble small points, but the facts survive.
engine.sense: Several wrong fits: "mate" addressed to the ladies, "have their mitts full" (the idiom is hands full, busy), "bugger all of a housekeeper" for "Not much of a housekeeper".
engine.authenticity: Stage-Australian inserts bolted onto American text: "Crikey, he gets up on a chair", "Anyway, Pulls his hand away", "grotty bloody awful quick", with "I guess" and "To be sure" left in.
engine.register: Largely untranslated ("I shouldn't say she had the homemaking instinct", "loyal to your sex"), with a few bolted-on words; well under level 4.
engine.tone: The scene's tension survives in the untouched lines, but "Crikey" in a stage direction and Mrs Hale's "my bloody kitchen" jar against it.
engine.flow: Broken joins: "Anyway, Pulls his hand away, sticky", "bugger all of a housekeeper, would you say, ladies, ay?", "grotty bloody awful quick".
engine.variety: Leans on the same fillers: "Anyway," three times, "mitts" three times, "bloody" stacked in.
engine.essence: Recognisably the original because most of it is the original, though flattened by the inserts.

summaries.yarn-troppo: A rich, mostly natural level-4 retelling that keeps the scene whole; a few stock lines and invented asides pull it toward pastiche.
summaries.unharnessed: Natural, faithful and well weighted; the best balance of voice and fidelity.
summaries.dinkum-3: Fluent and well pitched, but it reverses the towel line and drops "trifles".
summaries.yarn-dinkum: The most faithful candidate, natural where it changes things, but lighter than level 4.
summaries.engine: A rule-engine pass: mostly untranslated, with bolted-on fillers that break grammar and sense.
